Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to address Parliament on Monday, describing the UK's agreement with the EU as a "landmark" deal that offers what he calls a "very real prospect" of the next decade being considerably more prosperous than the preceding one. He will frame it as a choice between a broken status quo and change, and repeat his claim that it is "the single biggest growth measure to be delivered in this parliament," citing Treasury analysis suggesting it could add 0.5% to UK GDP—equivalent to £17bn—and he described the agreement on Friday as a win-win covering British food exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme. Burnham also asserts that polling indicates public support for closer EU ties and characterizes the deal as either easing cost-of-living pressure or allowing food prices to rise further.

However, this announcement drew sharp criticism from opposing political figures. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called the deal unfair because UK farmers would have to follow Brussels-made rules; she disputed Burnham's £17bn figure—accusing him of "plucking that figure out of the air"—and cited alternative modelling suggesting a 0.0% impact on GDP, which she attributed to the Treasury analysis he referenced.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage dismissed it as "a very good day for the EU," arguing closer ties would humiliate Britain and harm small firms through added red tape and compliance costs; he also called Burnham a fraud. Former prime ministers Theresa May—who urged him to move on—, Sir Tony Blair—who said rejoining should only happen if the EU reforms—and Rishi Sunak—who warned reopening the debate could become a distraction—all criticized the arrangement over the weekend.

On substance, Burnham noted that both sides would conduct an informal brainstorming process regarding the UK's long-term relationship with the EU. He acknowledged the deal was "probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament" and stated he wanted to inform Parliament afterward so decisions could be made about that future relationship.
items.title: Burnham to tell MPs 'landmark' EU deal could make next decade 'much better'

items.summary: Bereaved families across England, Wales, and Northern Ireland are borrowing money or forgoing memorial services because state funeral support no longer covers a typical funeral director's fee. The funeral expenses payment (FSP) provides cemetery or crematorium fees plus up to £1,000 for other costs; while the first element has kept pace with inflation, the £1,000 cap has been frozen since 2020 and is the only part of social security benefits not protected from losing value over time. Lindesay Mace, co-manager of Down to Earth (run by Quaker Social Action), reports that families cannot focus on grief due to financial stress while topping up payments, citing Carol, who received the benefit but was £1,000 short even for a simple funeral and is still raising money for her daughter's headstone. A recent report by the Social Security Advisory Committee found that had the cap risen with CPI it would now be worth about £1,300 instead of £1,000, while average costs for mortuary care, coffin, and hearse have reached £2,605 — meaning state help meets less than 40% of this bill. The report also notes the bereavement support payment (BSP), frozen since its 2017 introduction, has suffered substantial real-terms falls; the higher rate for claimants with children totals £9,800 (£3,500 lump sum plus up to 18 monthly payments of £350) rather than the £13,448 it would reach if increased in line with CPI. Terry Tennens, chief executive of the National Society of Allied and Independent Funeral Directors, warned that freezes push people toward unattended cremation because it is cheaper, eliminating a place to remember mourners. MPs are set to debate the BSP after a petition for annual uprating received more than 108,000 signatures, though a Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson maintained the payment was intended as short-term support with further help available through universal credit.
items.title: Frozen Funeral Benefit Payments Leave Bereaved Families in Debt

items.summary: Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham briefed MPs on a Friday deal with the EU, framing it as part of Keir Starmer's incrementalist approach rather than a victory. The agreement covers three areas—food and drink, emissions trading, and youth mobility—and its core provisions remain unratified because member states insist Britain resolve a dispute over tuition fees for European students before signing off; Burnham is described as determined to rejoin the EU but no progress is expected before the next general election. Negotiating with 27-member state club proved difficult: France and Italy issued a statement tying implementation to a tuition-fee deal, leading analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group to warn that incremental negotiation has reached its end and risks turning Britain into a 'cherrypicking state.' Beyond the summit itself, four structural factors shape rejoining prospects. Europe's far right has grown more than five times since the 1990s, with support rising sharply over the last three years; whether this makes membership less attractive may hinge on next year's French elections and Marine Le Pen, who is favored to win but could trigger a domestic crisis that strains EU-France relations. The EU's Made in Europe strategy uses public money to favor single-market goods and risks deindustrializing the UK car industry by excluding Britain from the scheme, though Friday promised closer steel and electric vehicle supply-chain cooperation. Finally, defense has become the strongest argument for rejoining as the EU shifts security into shared governance through its Security Action for Europe facility offering up to €150bn in loans; Britain refused its financial contribution but a deal may still emerge, even as an increasingly skeptical EU views the US as unreliable on security and challenges the UK's 'special relationship.' The analysis rests largely on Rahman's assessments of these trends. Limitations include that all core agreements are unratified, no rejoining progress is projected before the next election, and the piece treats Burnham's ambitions skeptically rather than confirming any concrete outcome.
items.title: Andy Burnham's EU reset and the obstacles to UK rejoining

items.summary:
A commentary by Amit John Kurien of RV University, Bengaluru argues that global studies on the drivers of deforestation inaccurately attribute forest loss to shifting cultivation (swidden farming), conflating land cover with land use and tree cover with forests. The author notes that estimating deforestation—defined as permanent conversion of forest to another land use—is only reliable when distinct land uses can be differentiated, yet influential mapping often coarsens spatial resolution by clustering land classes, trading accuracy for precision.

As supporting evidence, the commentary compares Philip Curtis et al.'s 2018 study (which ranked shifting agriculture as the second most important driver of global forest loss) with Andreas Heinimann et al.'s 2017 map of shifting cultivation. The authors found that approximately 4.5 million sq km—about 1.5 times the size of India—were misidentified globally as having shifting-agriculture-driven 'forest loss' despite no evidence in Heinimann's map, with two-thirds of this mismatch occurring in Africa.

The commentary attributes these errors partly to colonial-era framing that vilified shifting cultivation and led institutions like the FAO (1957) and post-colonial nations to stigmatize it; India's Wasteland Atlas classifies jhum as 'unproductive,' while Bangladesh and Myanmar use similar categories for land acquisition. The authors caution that misclassification has real-world consequences, enabling state or private takeover of communal upland lands used by millions of tribal farmers.

The commentary acknowledges these are the author's views drawn from published work with colleagues, and it does not provide quantitative estimates of actual shifting cultivation extent or forest loss—relying instead on map comparisons that identify mismatches rather than measuring true deforestation rates.
items.title: Why deforestation science gets shifting cultivation wrong

items.summary: A privately operated hydrogen station in Namie, Fukushima Prefecture—located along National Route 459 en route to Katsurao—is struggling financially as it attempts to remain operational. The site promotes its services through roadside signage advertising accessible fueling and free 30-minute test drives in fuel-cell vehicles. This case illustrates the broader financial difficulties confronting Japan's transition toward a hydrogen-powered economy, particularly within regions still rebuilding after the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and nuclear disaster.
items.title: Fukushima's Hydrogen Station Struggles Amid Financial Challenges

items.summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) announced on Monday that it suspended the licenses of five nutraceutical and health supplement manufacturers—Vedant Remedies, Lucid Health Care Pvt Ltd, Ambico Ayurvedic Healthcare, Vitamedic Health Nutraceuticals, and Adorreal Healthcare—for serious safety violations. Vedant Remedies was cited for poor hygiene, damaged infrastructure, lack of proper storage, expired food flavouring substances, and missing food safety records. Lucid Health Care's premises were found to have poor hygiene, inadequate lighting, improper storage, faulty pest control, and a failure to segregate Ayurvedic and nutraceutical products; handlers also lacked protective equipment and mandatory FoSTaC training, with food safety, testing, and maintenance records not properly maintained. Adorreal Healthcare's license was suspended because its licensed premises were non-operational due to ongoing construction while the company held an active FSSAI license against a disposed site and furnished false or misleading information; the suspension was issued under the Food Safety Act, 2006. Vitamedic Health Nutraceuticals shifted from its licensed premises without endorsement of the new address on its existing license, and the relocated premises were shared with another food processing unit engaged in meat processing (M/s Myyo Foods India Private Limited). Ambico Ayurvedic Healthcare's premises lacked hygiene, sanitation, and other compliance standards. The report was published on November 23, 2026.
items.title: FSSAI Suspends Licenses of Five Nutraceutical and Health Supplement Manufacturers Over Safety Violations

items.summary: James Brown, a 56-year-old house-hunter originally from the Midlands in England, moved approximately 10,000 miles (16,000km) from Australia to Tylorstown near Ferndale in Rhondda Cynon Taf after spotting a three-bedroom house listed at £80,000 online. He noted that an equivalent property in his home region would have cost around £200,000. Brown described the area as ideal for commuters with amenities nearby and characterized south Wales' affordability as 'unreal.' Ferndale is cited by Zoopla as Wales' most affordable town, with an average property price of £116,200; the site stated a typical home there costs less than twice the annual wages of two full-time workers. Despite these low prices, local residents report ongoing difficulty affording homes. Emma Weston, 36, who runs a café in Ferndale, said she chose to invest her savings in her business rather than buy property and noted that despite cheaper housing, the cost-of-living crisis makes everything expensive; her electrician partner also contributes income but they have no deposit available. Marcus, 31, took a job nearly 100 miles (165km) away in Somerset to afford a family home. Estate agent David Ricketts attributed low prices partly to outside buyers and buy-to-rent landlords drawn by reasonable rental yields that he expects to grow, though Brown acknowledged this influx may hinder local residents from purchasing. Donna Thomas, 41, rents with her partner and three children because mortgages are too costly; she expressed willingness for investors to purchase properties and rent them back to locals like herself. Chiropractor Ellie Thomas, 25, who lives with her parents in Ferndale while saving toward a deposit near a city, said the area lacks amenities and shops have closed, though she acknowledged buying elsewhere would be more expensive.
items.title: Man Relocates from Australia to Wales Over Low Property Prices While Locals Struggle to Afford Homes

items.summary: A seven-year-old boy was pulled alive from the rubble of a residential building in Dymer, in Ukraine's Kyiv region, approximately 14 hours after an overnight Russian strike. The attack occurred at around 05:00 local time while residents were asleep; Zelensky described it as striking the building and 'practically blowing a section of it to smithereens.' Overnight strikes on Dymer killed 11 people according to Ukrainian officials, though regional head Tymur Tkachenko earlier reported six injured with others still missing. A second person rescued alive was a 79-year-old woman receiving hospital treatment. In separate attacks in the Kyiv region, one more death occurred when a strike hit a private home in Bila Tserkva and set it ablaze, and Zelensky confirmed three killed and 13 wounded (with Mayor Illya Dikov noting three children among the injured) at a grocery store in Vyshneve. The rescued boy was reported to be in stable condition after being taken to hospital. Emergency operations involved more than 130 people, with Tkachenko stating rescuers would continue until they had 'complete information about every single person,' though Zelensky noted efforts were complicated by recurring air raid alerts and renewed threats. Vyhivskyi reported that more than 70 strikes had been launched across 10 Ukrainian regions as of Sunday evening, and Russia also struck a power substation in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
items.title: Boy Rescued After Russian Strike on Dymer, Kyiv Region

items.summary:
On November 22, under the guidance of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the Shanghai, Shenzhen, and Beijing Stock Exchanges along with China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Limited jointly unveiled a policy package aimed at stabilizing market expectations, bolstering the inherent stability of the A-share market, refining its institutional framework, and fostering a sound market ecosystem. The central event involved several coordinated measures across margin requirements, market structure reforms, and fee reductions.

The primary mechanism was an adjustment to counter-cyclical regulation of margin trading: with CSRC approval, the three bourses lowered the minimum margin ratio for margin purchases from 100% to 80%, effective November 30, 2026. This revision lifts the leverage ratio to 1.25 times and is estimated to unlock approximately 400 billion yuan ($59.9 billion) in incremental funds by cutting costs for new positions and revitalizing existing capital under margin contracts. The text notes that previous cuts in August 2023 and a hike in January 2026 both delivered their intended counter-cyclical outcomes, framing this adjustment as part of an established regulatory pattern.

A second mechanism involved the Shenzhen Stock Exchange launching public consultations on introducing a market-maker system for the ChiNext board. The rationale is that ChiNext's concentration of sci-tech innovation firms exposes stock prices to sizable swings from technological upgrades, sector sentiment, and overseas volatility; market makers would provide counter-directional quotes during turbulence as a "shock absorber," narrow bid-ask spreads, diversify participants, bring fresh capital into the market, boost investor confidence, and anchor expectations.

A third set of measures concerned fee reductions. The Shanghai Stock Exchange will waive trading unit usage fees and cut data center service charges, with 2026 total fee reductions projected to exceed 2.4 billion yuan (including an expected benefit of 1.368 billion yuan). The Shenzhen Stock Exchange's package includes waivers for trading unit usage and online voting service charges plus reductions in communication service fees, set to deliver 1.39 billion yuan in benefits with aggregate 2026 reductions topping 2.2 billion yuan. Additionally, China Securities Depository and Clearing Corporation Limited announced a temporary exemption of certain bond registration and settlement fees for corporate bond issuers of green enterprises, sci-tech innovation enterprises, and private enterprises from January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2028.

The text presents these figures as projections or estimates (e.g., "expected," "projected," "estimated") rather than realized outcomes. The market-maker system remains in the public consultation phase and is not yet implemented.
items.title: China Stock Exchanges Unveil Policy Package to Stabilize A-Share Market

items.summary:
Former Linq Buslines managers Rodney Parker (42) and Katie Parker (39) were convicted today in Gosford Local Court after pleading guilty to heavy vehicle safety breaches linked to the June 2023 crash that killed 10 people. Driver Brett Andrew Button, who admitted Tramadol dependence impaired his driving on the night of the accident, is serving a maximum of 32 years in jail.

Both managers faced a $59,000 fine but were ordered to pay only $7,000 each due to guilty pleas and limited financial means. Judge Kirralee Perry set these reduced fines after noting their constrained ability to pay more.

Katie Parker pleaded guilty to failing to take reasonable action on over-speed incidents and to failures relating to substance-use disclosures. She was reportedly told of Button's opioid use four months before the crash but made no further inquiries, despite her role in enforcing the company drug and alcohol policy. Judge Perry found she failed to investigate the medication's effects on driving.

In terms of speeding, Parker's monitoring role came under scrutiny: the court heard there was no specific speed disciplinary policy separate from a vehicle monitoring device, and non-conforming reports were completed weeks after over-speeds. The bus Button drove had an 18-tonne gross vehicle mass, exceeding New South Wales' 100 km/h limit for vehicles above 4.5 tonnes.

Rodney Parker pleaded guilty to failing to make adequate inquiries about Button's prior employment. He conducted a reference check via text message with casual language Judge Perry described as "cavalier, irresponsible, flippant and careless," including referring to drivers as "steering wheel attendants." The court heard recruitment failings occurred when Button was employed in November 2022, noting the company had no policy requiring medical assessments or valid references.

The crash followed Linq Buslines' August fine of $650,000 for safety breaches including over-speeding, poor recruitment checks, and employing a drug-impaired driver. Directors Christopher Fogg and Anthony Royle were each fined $12,000 in that case but are appealing their convictions.

Linq Buslines has since collapsed, with ASIC reporting only $265,000 in cash as of October 19, expected to be depleted once administrators were paid.
items.title: Two Linq Buslines Managers Fined for Safety Failings in Deadly Hunter Wedding Crash

items.summary: A reader presents a ranked list of non-fiction books read during 2026, ordered by the sequence in which they were finished. The collection spans twelve titles covering World War II history (Alan Allport's "Advance Britannia" and Vasily Grossman's "From the Front Line," both focusing on 1941-1945), literary biography (Anna Arno's "Paul Celan: A Life"), economic history, artificial intelligence (Sebastian Mallaby's work on DeepMind), Soviet history, Native American history, medieval manuscripts, philosophy of mind, Roman and early Christian history, child development, Russian imperial history, and a broad survey of civilization. The author notes that 2026 offered fewer non-fiction titles than most years, attributing this to what appears to be a publishing market recession for intelligent non-fiction, though the author expresses uncertainty about whether niche personal interests are also a contributing factor; Jonathan Parshall's "1942: Crux of War" was read only partially due to its length. The author's top recommendation is Anna Arno's biography of Paul Celan, which Henry Oliver reviewed favorably as one of the best works of literary non-fiction published that year and praised for its mastery of detail, sensitivity to poetry, and controlled narrative style in handling difficult subject matter; however, this endorsement reflects a reviewer's opinion rather than an objective assessment. The author also indicates plans to publish addenda covering books released between now and year's end.
items.title: Author's List of Best Non-Fiction Books Read in 2026

items.summary: This Monday newsletter from Euronews's Leo Cendrowicz reports on a week in which diplomatic activity intensified while Russia's war in Ukraine showed no sign of slowing. The European Commission is set to unveil its 22nd sanctions package against Russia, targeting the country's banks, cryptocurrency platforms, and shadow fleet along with third-country companies supplying blacklisted goods; it would be the first package since the Commission established a dedicated sanctions office aiming to bring together 50 to 60 staff. The timing coincides with preparations for multilateral peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine, the US, and Europe, though European capitals largely view Moscow as having little interest in serious negotiations. On the military front, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Russia launched around 2,700 drones, nearly 1,460 aerial bombs, and 165 missiles over a week, striking 20 Ukrainian regions; Ukraine also claimed attacks on Russian vessels in Libya and the Gulf of Finland without attribution. NATO grew concerned after three Russian cruise missiles violated Polish airspace during multinational exercises involving British troops, prompting Poland to seek additional support for its eastern border while NATO chief Mark Rutte pledged to defend allied territory. Separately, COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya, Turkey, ending as the biggest failure of UN climate diplomacy since Copenhagen in 2009 after oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia resisted reaffirming fossil fuel transition commitments and promoting carbon capture technologies; EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra warned that multilateralism was in 'dire straits.' The newsletter also covers a budget dispute over European Council President António Costa's proposal to cut €204 billion—more than 10%—from the Commission's original €2 trillion plan, which would include €8 billion from cohesion funds and anger 17 countries while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz argued the cuts go too far; Costa also floated a Big Tech tax potentially raising €5 billion annually. Finally, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was welcomed back to Brussels for talks with Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa on resetting post-Brexit relations, though Reform UK's Nigel Farage criticized him as betraying Brexit voters.
items.title: EU Sanctions, Ukraine Escalation, and COP Collapse Mark a Turbulent Week for Europe

items.summary:
On Sunday, 22 November, the Avenue des Champs-Élysées began its end-of-year festive season by switching on traditional Christmas lights. The installation spans fifty-two kilometres across four hundred trees using two million LEDs, with the event attended by Paris mayor Emmanuel Grégoire and patron Cate Blanchett. Illuminations run until 4 January 2027, featuring a five-minute light-and-sound show in three scenes—Awakening of Nature, Arrival of Winter, and Starry Night—every quarter hour between 5 p.m. and 1 a.m., with hourly silvery tones synchronized to the Eiffel Tower's display across the Seine.

The year also marks the return of the Paris Christmas market after ten years away, with two hundred exhibitors in wooden chalets between the Rond-Point des Champs-Élysées and Place de la Concorde. Per specifications, food chalets offer fully organic flour, French meat and mulled wine, plus a vegetarian option; Marc-Antoine Jamet, secretary general of LVMH and president of the Comité des Champs-Élysées, stated that 80% of offerings will be made in France, with an introduced Fabriqué à Paris label. The market includes a skating rink, fairground ride, Santa's House, a monumental reindeer, and around twenty scenographic installations.

Jamet framed the lights and market as matters of image and attractiveness for shopkeepers, noting that 14.3 million visitors strolled the avenue in 2025 to view them. The show replaced loud Christmas carols with music played via mobile phones, and the family-run company 2A from Nantes now organizes the market after Marcel Campion was permanently barred by court decision in 2017 over product and entertainment quality.

The Comité des Champs-Élysées expressed optimism about maintaining a calm atmosphere despite ongoing French demonstrations against school conditions and cost of living. Although the prefecture has not yet authorized marches on the avenue, it remains a symbolic protest site; as of publication, contact with Paris's prefect was reported to be regular.
items.title: Champs-Élysées Launches Christmas Lights and Revives Paris Christmas Market

items.summary: The South Australian government announced that public primary schools will restrict classroom screen time beginning next year, as part of a broader state effort to reduce children's device use. Laptops and tablets are banned for reception through Year 2 students across all public primary schools statewide, while a six-month trial introducing a weekly 'screen-free day' is set to launch at 10 sites covering Years 3 to 6 next year. These restrictions coincide with the phasing out of the bring-your-own-device (BYOD) program; Education Minister Lucy Hood stated that any screen use from Year 3 upward must serve a direct educational purpose, such as creating or learning collaboratively rather than 'mindless scrolling.' The government also cited handwriting improvement as a factor in its revised approach and introduced the 'Premier's Pen Licence' for Year 3 and Year 4 students. Exemptions will apply to students with disability, additional learning needs, and those at the School of the Air.
items.title: South Australia to Restrict Screen Time in Public Primary Schools

items.summary:
Chinese authorities announced that an official identified only by the surname Ma was sentenced to death for spying for a foreign intelligence service, with the penalty accompanied by a lifetime deprivation of political rights and forfeiture of all personal property. The case was publicized through a Monday post on WeChat's Baomiguan account, linked to the National Administration of State Secret Protection, as an admonition against leaking state secrets.

According to the post, Ma met a foreign intelligence officer named Kailin while stationed overseas and provided sensitive information including an internal telephone directory. He was later introduced to another officer, Tang Zheng, who threatened to report his prior illegal conduct unless he cooperated; Ma then agreed to supply confidential material using a dedicated laptop in exchange for more than 1 million yuan.

The announcement appears amid heightened attention to espionage involving China, following the March 2025 disclosure of a death sentence against former research institute employee Liu for espionage and illegally providing state secrets. The text also notes Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia CEO this month after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The post did not name the foreign agency involved, disclose when the incident occurred, or reveal Ma's rank.
items.title: China Sentences Official to Death for Espionage

items.summary:
A review into the UK's personal independence payment (Pip) led by disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has recommended a 'fundamental overhaul' of the assessment process, which he described as no longer fit for purpose. Writing in The Times ahead of the full report due Tuesday, Timms proposed that people with the most severe conditions and end-of-life care receive a less burdensome fast-track process to free up capacity for other cases. He argued that individuals with lifelong or degenerative illnesses should not face regular reassessments he characterized as adversarial and unnecessary. The review attributes the need for reform to marked shifts in disability over 13 years, including substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions alongside changes to society and the workplace.

The Timms review follows a separate Milburn review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets), which recommended scrapping Pip for under-25s. The government accepted those recommendations to move 18-to-24-year-olds onto an entirely new benefits system, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested the same philosophy could apply across all age ranges; however, it remains unclear how the two reviews will complement one another.

The review comes after a U-turn from Sir Keir Starmer's government on plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments by £5bn annually. More than 130 MPs, including 120 Labour members, signed an amendment rejecting those cuts in 2025 over fears of pushing people into relative poverty.

Pip is projected to cost more than £41bn by 2030, up from £15bn in 2020, and was claimed by 4m UK residents as of 30 April 2026 per the Department for Work and Pensions. Disability charities have warned against weakening Pip, with Scope's executive director James Taylor noting that life costs more when disabled and describing the payment as vital financial support.
items.title: Timms Review Calls for Fundamental Overhaul of Personal Independence Payment Assessments

items.summary: An Indonesian company, PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama, sought to register a captive-breeding facility with the Secretariat of CITES in August so it could commercially breed and export rare Asian golden cats (Catopuma temminckii) as pets. If approved, it would become the first facility worldwide to do so for the international pet market; signatory countries had until Nov. 10 to object before the company was added to the registry of commercial breeding facilities. The CITES register does not yet list PT Alam Nusantara Jayatama for Asian golden cats, and Mongabay reported that it contacted the Secretariat to confirm whether objections were received but has not gotten a response. Classified as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List with an estimated 7,000 individuals remaining in the wild, the species is threatened by habitat loss and poaching for skins and bones; wild-caught animals are protected under CITES Appendix I, while captive-bred animals from registered facilities can be legally exported. According to documents from Indonesia's Ministry of Forestry submitted to CITES, the facility began breeding in 2013 with four legally acquired wild-caught cats and reported a population of 36 individuals across three generations by 2025. Conservation experts questioned both this reproduction rate and animal welfare standards: Mike Brocklehurst, a carnivore specialist who ran an Asian golden cat conservation program at Melbourne Zoo, said the species is difficult to breed in captivity—males often kill females upon introduction—and that reaching the claimed breeding numbers likely relies on hand-rearing kittens pulled early from their mothers. Sandra Reichler, curator for mammals at Heidelberg Zoo and head of EAZA's breeding program, noted that early separation causes behavioral deficits and criticized the company's 9-square-meter (97-square-foot) enclosures as far below EAZA's recommended minimum of 150 m² (1,615 ft²). Chris Shepherd of the Center for Biological Diversity said commercial captive breeding rarely reduces wild demand and often hinders conservation. Neither Alam Nusantara Jayatama nor owner Danny Gunalen responded to Mongabay by publication.
items.title: Indonesia's proposed captive-breeding facility for Asian golden cats faces CITES review amid conservation concerns

items.summary: On Monday, Nov. 23, oil prices remained nearly flat during Asian trading despite ongoing Middle East conflict, with Brent crude rising just 10 cents (0.11%) to $92.67 a barrel and US WTI gaining 16 cents (0.19%) to $83.57 by 0423 GMT. The modest gains reflected a risk premium that investors priced in as shipping and refinery attacks persisted, even amid diplomatic efforts to end the war; Brent had earlier fallen $1 to $91.57 before WTI hit a session low of $82.63. This calm contrasted with prior volatility, as both benchmarks declined sharply last week—Brent 4% and WTI 5%. The fighting from an unresolved US-Israeli war against Iran continued underpinning prices: the Houthi movement claimed it struck a Saudi Arabian oil refinery on Sunday, UK Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on Gulf shipping near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, Bahrain said an Iranian attack hit a civilian industrial facility Saturday, and Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed they launched a missile-and-drone assault on US military positions in the kingdom. Analyst Vandana Hari of Vanda Insights characterized a tense US-Iran stalemate as increasingly likely through year-end while noting Trump could still shift toward renewed military action; she added that fluctuating threats and rhetoric would keep driving a marginal geopolitical risk premium, holding prices broadly rangebound unless either side escalated further.
items.title: Oil Holds in Tight Range as Gulf Attacks Sustain Risk Premium

items.summary:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has broadened its inspection of packaged drinking water brands after laboratory tests detected harmful substances in a sample from Bisleri International. Prosecution was initiated following these findings, while samples were also collected from numerous other manufacturers, including counterfeit brands; results for those remain pending.

Bisleri clarified that the contamination involved only a specific batch sourced from Goa and asserted its bottled water is safe overall. The company noted differences between packaged drinking water and mineral water in response to the notice.

The text presents these claims as reported statements rather than independently verified facts, with FSSAI emphasizing ongoing testing to ensure compliance with safety standards and protect public health. No specific details on the nature or concentration of harmful substances were provided.
items.title: FSSAI Expands Inspections of Packaged Drinking Water Brands After Bisleri Sample Found Unsafe

items.summary:
According to an exchange filing reported by Economic Times (written by Surbhi Khanna, who is not a SEBI-registered research analyst), Ashoka Buildcon secured two contracts from the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and the Jaipur Metro. The company's shares rose 7% following these announcements.

The first contract was for Rs 1,465 crore (excluding GST) to build an 8-lane, access-controlled stretch of the Vadodara-Mumbai Expressway spanning 35.4 km from Jujuwa to Gandeva in Gujarat under EPC mode, with a defect liability period of 10 years and completion scheduled within 18 months.

The second contract was for Rs 1,628 crore to design and construct an elevated viaduct and 11 elevated stations as part of Jaipur Metro Phase-II MRTS Package 4 (Khasa Kothi/Phase-I), with a completion timeline of 36 months. The company clarified that neither its promoters nor group companies have any interest in the entities that awarded either contract.

On performance, Ashoka Buildcon shares gained 10.37% over the past week and 20.82% over the past month, but declined 29.12% this calendar year and 33.34% over the past year; over three years they fell 14.23%, while gaining 18.64% in the past five years.

The article notes that its views should not be construed as recommendations of Economic Times, and readers are advised to base investment decisions on their own assessment.

items.summary: Leaders of the Samajwadi Party and Congress met in New Delhi at senior Congress leader Pramod Tiwari's residence to negotiate seat-sharing arrangements ahead of the upcoming Uttar Pradesh assembly election, with talks reportedly progressing cordially. The two parties hold differing negotiation priorities: Congress intends to leverage its 2024 Lok Sabha results, while the Samajwadi Party emphasizes assembly-level outcomes and seat winnability. During this period, Congress MP Imran Masood criticized a BJP campaign slogan. The source text is accompanied by unrelated items—including a Tamil Nadu controversy over Karthigai Deepam lighting following Supreme Court permission, a Bisleri water safety clarification after a Goa batch notice, Prime Minister Modi's bilateral talks with Nepalese PM Balendra Shah on trade and connectivity, and an investigation into mercury-laced fairness cream causing kidney damage in Kerala—none of which relate to the alliance negotiations. The text presents these as reported events without independent verification.
items.title: Samajwadi Party and Congress Begin Alliance Negotiations for Uttar Pradesh Assembly Election

items.summary: The Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay began replacing ceiling fan rods with wall-mounted fans in Hostel 4 on November 22, two months after a second-year student allegedly died by suicide there on September 18. The replacement was announced via an email from the general secretary for students' affairs and is intended to be extended to other hostels in phases over time. IIT Bombay framed the work as part of broader efforts to improve hostel safety and infrastructure, while also examining options such as student feedback surveys and consultations with representatives. Protesting students at the campus Justice Corner criticized the move, arguing that no scientific study establishes ceiling fan rods as a primary means of suicide and that the premise is illogical for a research institute to promote. The students called instead for structural accountability on academic pressure, caste- and gender-based discrimination, and inadequate channels for raising concerns, while urging the Student Council not to be co-opted into producing symbolic responses.
items.title: IIT Bombay Begins Replacing Ceiling Fan Rods After Student Suicide

items.summary:
The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the UN Climate Change Convention, held in Antalya, Türkiye, concluded on Sunday without reaching consensus on its cover decision. India's Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav confirmed that no pact was adopted because the European Union and other nations disagreed with oil-dependent economies such as Saudi Arabia over phasing out fossil fuels. The conference ran two days past its scheduled Friday end date.

The EU, backed by more than 130 countries (per AFP), insisted any agreement include a provision to phase out fossil fuels; Panama, Vanuatu, and the Marshall Islands joined this stance. Oil-producing states opposed including such language in the final deal. Because UN decisions require consensus, opposition from even one country is sufficient to block an agreement.

At COP30 in Brazil last year, the EU and more than 80 other countries had called for a fossil fuel phase-out roadmap but withdrew that demand after oil-dependent economies gained support from major powers including India and China. Those nations advocated instead for a phase-down—reducing rather than eliminating fossil fuels entirely—citing economic dependence on coal and petrol.

After the talks, Yadav said India remained committed to dialogue while raising concerns about historical emissions consuming a disproportionate share of the global carbon budget and calling for equity and climate justice. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed disappointment at the lack of consensus, and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese attributed the failure to difficult geopolitical times.

The last similar outcome occurred at COP15 in Copenhagen (2009), where negotiations aimed at a new agreement were not finalized until six years later in Paris.
items.title: COP31 Ends Without Agreement Over Fossil Fuel Phase-Out

items.summary: Seat-sharing negotiations between the Samajwadi Party (SP) and the Congress for Uttar Pradesh's 2027 Assembly elections formally began in Delhi on Monday with a brief first-round meeting between four-member panels from each party. The talks, described as taking place in a 'cordial atmosphere,' focused on finalizing an agenda and seat-allocation approach across the state's 403 Assembly constituencies. SP panel head Ram Gopal Yadav stated that both parties listened to one another's points of view and would complete the process within two to three days, with further meetings scheduled for subsequent days. Congress representatives echoed this positive tone: UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said an agreement is 'nearly settled,' while Aradhana Misra (Mona) expressed confidence that finalization could occur within two to four days and emphasized that the formula would be based on winnability rather than rigid numbers. Congress MP Pramod Tiwari noted both sides were examining constituency-wise strengths and data, with additional meetings possible if required. The SP panel comprises Ram Gopal Yadav, state president Shyam Lal Pal, Ghosi Lok Sabha MP Rajiv Rai, and Kairana Lok Sabha MP Iqra Chaudhary (Iqra Hasan). The Congress panel includes UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam, state president Aradhana Mishra (Mona), state working president Imran Masood, and AICC general secretary KC Venugopal. These structured panels mark a formal start to opposition coordination within the INDIA bloc ahead of 2027. The Congress had earlier indicated interest in contesting around 181 constituencies, while the SP maintained that allocation must rest on local strength, past performance, and realistic winning prospects—reflecting the party's dominance after it won 111 seats versus two for Congress in the 2022 Assembly elections. The first phase (November 23–24) would examine constituencies individually to avoid vote division against the BJP while maximizing overall tally.
items.title: Samajwadi Party and Congress Begin Formal UP Seat-Sharing Talks for 2027 Elections

items.summary: In the domestic market, MCX silver futures for December 2026 delivery rose Rs 3,600 (2.5%) to Rs 1,51,390 per kg after a 4-day fall, while gold futures for the same month climbed Rs 2,800 (2.3%) to Rs 1,24,550 per 10 grams, snapping a 5-day losing streak. The price movements occurred against a backdrop of ongoing speculation about US Federal Reserve monetary policy: Fed Governor Lisa Cook argued on Friday that the current rate was insufficient to address inflation she described with "great concern," while ECB member Alvaro Santos Pereira noted persistent energy-related inflation pressures from rising natural gas prices, though their spread across the euro zone remained unclear. Markets were pricing a 93% probability of an interest rate hike at the Fed's December meeting per CME's FedWatch tool; higher rates generally raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding assets like gold and silver, making them less attractive to investors. On international markets, spot gold rose 1.2% to $3,576.10 per ounce by 0048 GMT after recovering from Friday's decline—its lowest since September 2025—and following a roughly 9% weekly drop, its steepest since March; spot silver gained 2.3% to $42.11, platinum advanced 1.4% to $1,316.97, and palladium climbed 1.3% to $904.15. Manoj Kumar Jain of Prithvi Finmart (an SEBI-registered research analyst) characterized gold and silver as deeply oversold, suggesting any positive Fed signals could trigger a sharp recovery while warning of continued volatility driven by crude oil prices, the dollar index, and rate-hike concerns; he set technical support/resistance levels for both metals on international and MCX markets. He advised long-term investors to accumulate via SIPs during the correction but cautioned traders against fresh long positions until stability returns. Physical gold rates in Indian cities ranged from Rs 91,712/8 grams (standard) to Rs 1,00,176/8 grams (pure), with Delhi slightly higher than Mumbai, Chennai, and Hyderabad. The article's price movements are reported facts, but the trading recommendations reflect only Jain's individual views as an analyst; readers were advised that these should not be construed as ETMarkets' own guidance.
items.title: MCX Gold and Silver Prices Rise After Recent Declines Amid Fed Rate-Hike Speculation

items.summary: A 17-year-old girl in Kerala's Areekode police jurisdiction alleged that using a fairness cream marketed as 'F Tune' caused serious health complications, including kidney damage. The teenager reportedly discovered the product through Instagram advertisements promising to clear pimples and pigmentation while giving skin a glowing appearance; she ordered it via WhatsApp and used it for nearly a year before developing what doctors at Aster MIMS Mother Hospital described as a serious kidney condition requiring treatment costing about Rs 1 lakh (approximately $12,000). Laboratory tests cited by the treating physicians detected mercury levels of 12,500 parts per million in the cream, far exceeding the permissible limit of less than 1 ppm. The complaint alleges that the producer knew of the health risks associated with excessive mercury yet continued selling it. Police registered a case under sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, and the Kerala Police Act after the teenager's complaint from Ugrapuram, naming the cream's producer as an accused while further investigation continues.
items.title: Kerala teen alleges kidney damage from mercury-laced fairness cream as state launches crackdown on fake cosmetics

items.summary:
Daikin has introduced a replacement technology for its R-32-based Mini VRV 5 S-series heat pumps, allowing existing variable refrigerant volume (VRV) and variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems that use R-410A refrigerant to be upgraded to R-32 equipment while retaining the existing refrigerant piping and wiring. According to Daikin, this retrofit shortens installation time by up to 22% and reduces capital expenditure by up to 55% compared with a complete system replacement, alongside energy savings of up to 16% versus equivalent R-410A systems.

The new Mini VRV 5 RXYSA-B range is offered in three sizes—4 HP, 5 HP, and 6 HP—and uses R-32 refrigerant with a global warming potential (GWP) of 675, approximately 68% lower than that of R-410A. The existing Mini VRV 5 S-series platform provides nominal cooling capacities from 12.1 kW to 15.5 kW and rated heating capacities from 8.4 kW to 10.7 kW depending on the model, with maximum heating capacities reaching 18 kW under specified test conditions.

The outdoor units feature a compact single-fan design measuring 869 mm in height, low-noise operation down to 39 dB(A), and support for total piping lengths of up to 300 meters. The systems also incorporate Daikin's Shîrudo refrigerant safety technology—integrated leak detection sensors, audible and visual alarms, and automatic shut-off valves—to facilitate the use of mildly flammable R-32 in occupied buildings; these factory-integrated measures reportedly support compliance with IEC 60335-2-40.

A stated limitation is that the technical specifications refer to the existing RXYSA-A platform, as detailed performance data for the newly introduced RXYSA-B replacement models have not yet been confirmed.
items.title: Daikin Launches R-32 Retrofit Solution for Existing Residential Heat Pump Series

items.summary: Union Minister of State for Petroleum and Natural Gas Suresh Gopi questioned the testing methodology used by the Karnataka government to detect ethanol content in petrol, dismissing concerns over fuel with higher-than-prescribed ethanol levels. In response to reports that tests found 27% and 28% ethanol—exceeding prescribed standards—Gopi called these reported figures 'unacceptable' and raised doubts about whether samples were collected directly from refineries rather than at retail outlets. He argued that fuel passes through multiple stages, including transportation and storage in underground tanks at retail points, which are not currently monitored or sealed by the government. Gopi maintained that oil companies bear responsibility for complying with Union regulations and that periodic checks ensure adherence to standards, while insisting the issue should not be politicized. Defending E20 fuel more broadly, he cited Paraguay and Brazil as examples of higher blending levels and stated India's blending percentage could rise to 30% or 40% in future, contingent on scientific assessments and regulatory requirements. He also rejected claims that consumers are being compelled to use E20 petrol, asserting people retain the choice not to purchase it. The minister acknowledged Kerala's right to conduct its own tests but indicated central authorities would submit their own reports for legal resolution.
items.title: Suresh Gopi Questions Karnataka's E20 Testing and Defends Ethanol Blending

items.summary:
A global sell-off in gold—driven primarily by forced liquidation of debt-heavy, overvalued AI stocks (US tech logged its worst session since COVID the same week Anthropic raised $81.3 billion on a 17 per cent surge) and fears of central-bank rate hikes—drove international prices down nearly 10 per cent in one week from January's record of $5,594.82 per ounce (about $180 per gram). While Asian markets saw sharp cuts, physical demand surged in India and China; silver fell over 60 per cent from its January peak while gold dropped more than 30 per cent globally. The correction is playing out unevenly across India: mutual-fund and ETF investors face large unrealized losses, exchange traders hit by margin calls, but wedding-season jewellery buyers benefit from cheaper prices amid a boom in showroom activity.

The article disputes Prime Minister Narendra Modi's claim that his earlier appeal to avoid non-essential gold purchases caused the domestic price correction. It notes international prices fell over 30 per cent from January's record versus Modi comparing only one day before his announcement, and that the reversal began in January 2026—before any government exhortation. In May, import duties on gold and silver were more than doubled (from 6 per cent to 15 per cent) partly to curb imports and support the rupee. World Gold Council data show India's market is a volume-and-value story: demand fell 12 per cent to 444 tonnes in nine months, yet value rose 38 per cent to Rs.6,688 billion ($71 billion), because high prices limited quantities but not total spending.

The most pressing risk stems from gold-financing NBFCs—Muthoot Finance, IIFL Finance, Bajaj Finance, and Manappuram Finance—which reported increased stage 2 assets (early stress or delinquency) as defaults loom for both lenders and their customers. The piece concludes that while the short term may offer some buyers a window of opportunity, prolonged price damage threatens Indian households already burdened by loans and rising costs; it likens Modi's self-attribution to "fool's gold," cautioning readers to distinguish real accomplishments from bogus claims.
items.title: Gold's Global Sell-Off Overshadowed by AI Volatility and Debunking of Modi Credit

items.summary: The fifth Mercom Capital–hosted Startup Pitch Competition, held in partnership with RE+, featured ten renewable energy startups pitching to a three-judge panel of Stephanie Annerose (director of investments at HASI), Alexander Carbone (vice president at Clairvest), and Raj Prabhu (CEO of Mercom Capital Group). The finalists spanned solar installation robotics—Cosmic Robotics' tracked, battery-electric Cosmic-1 robot reportedly places panels with ±5 mm precision while a three-person crew installs 400–500+ modules daily; O&M Robotics' SolTrek system that cleans up to 15,000 panels per day at ≥99% efficiency using ZeroWeight technology—EV charging optimization (evPower.ai's AI reportedly achieving 98.5% prediction accuracy with 20% higher energy sales and a 40% reduction in demand charges), smart home load management (Noble Carbon), data center solar-storage construction platforms (Axentum, Matrix Power Inc.), rooftop racking systems (SWIF Rack's UL 2703-certified solution), regulatory intelligence software (Fordje covering over 28,000 U.S. jurisdictions and retrieving 80–300 documents per jurisdiction in ~30 seconds for feasibility reports), grid cybersecurity gateways (LexaVolt), and power conversion technology combining energy routers with solid-state transformers. Raj Prabhu characterized the cohort as tackling pressing market challenges. Magnefy, a California-based finalist offering noninvasive transformer fault detection, won RE+ Start-Up of the Year after reporting >98% accuracy in classifying partial-discharge faults during controlled testing and targeting monitoring costs about one-tenth those of incumbent systems; it received a Mercom Capital communications package and an RE+ 2027 booth. The reported figures are self-reported by each company, and no independent verification or outcome data beyond the competition results is provided.
items.title: Ten Renewable Energy Startups Pitch at Mercom Capital's RE+ Startup Competition

items.summary: This news roundup reports on several events as of November 23, 2026, with the most prominent being US President Donald Trump's stated inclination to resume military strikes against Iran after the New Year if negotiations fail. According to Fox News, Trump said indirect talks with Tehran were ongoing but expressed frustration over lack of progress, describing Iranian negotiators dismissively and warning that vessels attempting to breach a US naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz would be attacked and sunk. The remarks come amid continued Iranian attacks on oil tankers despite the blockade. Separately, Libya's eastern-based government filed formal complaints with the UN General Assembly and Security Council seeking an investigation into drone boat attacks on Russian and Maltese ships off Benghazi; its parliament-appointed head Osama Hammad called for Ukraine to explain alleged military activities in Libya. The COP31 climate summit in Antalya closed without agreement after President Murat Kurum announced a proposed decision had not been adopted, criticizing some countries for lacking flexibility. In US politics, Democrats secured 258 seats in the House following November 3 midterms—attributed by the Associated Press as their strongest performance since before 1992—with gains of 44 seats nationwide; this total was reached after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Virginia Foxx in North Carolina's 5th District following a recount, with Hubbard leading by 330 votes out of approximately 287,000 cast. The article notes these figures are reported claims from Fox News and AP rather than independently verified facts.

items.summary: Early Sunday morning drone strikes hit residential areas and a United Nations building in Sudan's capital, Khartoum, between 2 a.m. and 4:30 a.m. local time, damaging homes near the airport and other parts of the city while one house was reportedly completely destroyed. A witness described finding victims inside a damaged home with serious injuries to their hands, chest, and head, characterizing the targeting as indiscriminate since people could be struck whether asleep or moving about. Residents expressed concern over civilians seeking shelter amid ongoing violence, noting that many had been searching for safe housing before being hit by drones. The United Nations confirmed its premises were damaged while UN personnel inside and condemned the risks posed to humanitarian workers in civilian areas. These attacks occur within a war between Sudan's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces that began in April 2023, triggering widespread displacement, hunger, and a humanitarian crisis. Both sides have increasingly relied on drones, with the United Nations warning that such attacks are taking an escalating toll on civilians, including children.
items.title: Drone Strikes Damage Homes and UN Premises in Khartoum

items.summary: Following the International Court of Justice verdict on November 19 finding Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya, Noorul Amin—a 26-year-old Rohingya refugee who arrived in India at age eight—expressed hope that the ruling would lead to more humane treatment for refugees living in India. The ICJ found that Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State killed an estimated 10,000 Rohingya and prompted at least seven lakh (700,000) of them to flee to Bangladesh; it also noted decades of discriminatory measures that eroded the group's political and civil rights. Amin arrived via a makeshift boat built from bamboo in 2007 after his family fled what he described as a bloodbath, while his wife Zahida crossed into India on foot in 2020 at nearly age 18; both families had faced persecution since the early 2010s. Despite holding UN refugee cards—which have been issued by the UN since 2011—Amin's family experienced repeated detentions, including a five-month detention for him and his wife in Madanpur Khader after their arrest in 2020, while his parents spent three years detained. In May 2025, amid an Indian crackdown on 'Bangladeshi migrants' following the Pahalgam terror attack, Amin's family was among roughly 40 Rohingya flown to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands before being forced off a navy vessel into the sea toward Myanmar; his parents were never returned. India is not a signatory to UN refugee law or protocols and maintains that existing foreigner laws suffice. On economic grounds, Amin reported struggling to earn enough for rent of Rs 5,000–6,000 per month, sometimes skipping meals. Sabber Kyaw Min of the Rohingya Human Rights Initiative cited an estimated 22,000 Rohingya refugees in India as of latest figures. Amin's family had secured U.S. visas through UN resettlement but were blocked after Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and imposed travel restrictions; he also noted that Indian courts dismissed petitions against the deportations, with one bench calling it a 'beautifully crafted story.' The account reflects one refugee's perspective on India's policies and does not represent verified official statistics or comprehensive coverage of all Rohingya experiences.
items.title: Rohingya Refugee Hopes ICJ Genocide Verdict Will Improve India's Treatment of Refugees

items.summary: Companies active in alternative energy and related technology have criticized the European Union for plans to reduce the size of the European Competitiveness Fund as part of a broader budget cut. A group representing 75 companies and industry associations, including France's EDF, argued via a letter that the fund is essential for European businesses to compete with China and the United States in key industries (Reuters). At the end of last week, Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, proposed cutting the bloc's budget by €40 billion (~$44 billion) for 2028-2034 from an earlier Irish presidency proposal. However, compared to the European Commission's original budget proposal, Costa's version would shrink the budget by a much larger €180.6 billion (Reuters). The debate centers on competitiveness: critics blame EU-level energy policies for higher costs that undermine industry, while supporters argue accelerating the transition from hydrocarbons to low-carbon electricity could enhance competitiveness. The European Parliament also opposed the cuts; chief budget negotiator Siegfried Muresan called the proposal unacceptable and stated it cannot form the basis for consent, describing the EU budget as an investment budget rather than a strategy of repeated cuts (Reuters). In response, the energy company group insisted on boosting the fund by €26.6 billion to support industrial decarbonization and accelerated buildout of wind, solar, and battery storage.
items.title: EU Green Energy Giants Slam €40 Billion Budget Cut

items.summary:
The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, concluded two days after its scheduled end without reaching an agreement on the cover text. The primary sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels from draft texts; Saudi Arabia and Russia blocked any reference to them, while Australia and Turkey proposed dropping fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification with maximum clean energy use. This compromise drew backlash from the European Union along with Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text. The EU led a revolt that shattered the consensus needed to adopt the Turkish-Australian-proposed text.

The article notes this rejection does not signal an end to the COP process or the Paris Agreement, as these texts are non-binding political add-ons rather than formal requirements. However, it may indicate international climate cooperation will look different going forward. Fossil fuels remained unmentionable in official outcomes despite being explicitly addressed three years earlier at COP28 in Dubai with a transition-away commitment.

In response to the deadlock, Brazil launched a global fossil fuel phase-out roadmap outside the formal agenda that attracted support from India, Germany, and Nigeria, while EU member states are developing similar roadmaps. Frustration is likely to drive more nations toward informal channels: 57 nations attended a first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia earlier this year, with another meeting planned for next year co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Leadership figures avoided fossil fuel commitments—Turkish President Erdoğan announced two new Turkish oilfields while Australian PM Albanese made no commitment to halt new coal and gas projects. Both leaders emphasized the "35 by 35" electrification pledge, aiming to raise electricity's share of final energy use from about 23% currently to 35% by 2035; more than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on outside official negotiations.

As an "implementation COP," the summit focused on existing pledges. Developed nations called for faster emissions cuts while developing nations cited insufficient financial support, with African countries stressing that implementation is meaningless without actual resources from rich nations. Progress was achieved in supporting a just transition via a phased approach and improving alignment in climate adaptation, but broader efforts on the Global Goal on Adaptation remained unresolved.

On finance, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra had warned talks were "dead in the water" before the summit; no concrete progress occurred toward tripling adaptation funds pledged at COP30. Australia flagged boosting the Pacific climate fund, which ended A$450 million short of its $749 million 2026 target after rich nations merely re-announced existing pledges. The most notable pledge came from Solomon Islands PM Matthew Wale's commitment of $600,000 to the Green Climate Fund.

Climate science was unusually prominent; a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries obstructed IPCC report publication, and this marked the first UN summit since confirmation that the world will overshoot 1.5°C by 2030. With cover text support collapsing, statements supporting release of latest climate science were not approved—only technical conclusions expressing concern about increasing impacts remained.

Australia oversaw negotiations as president between 195 countries and the EU; Climate Minister Chris Bowen declared Australia had left "nothing on the field" after facing unbridgeable red lines. Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed powerful fossil fuel interests, while some nations called for reform of voting processes—though any such change would itself require consensus.

The article frames the collapse as potentially a catalyst rather than pure failure: former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres characterized more than 130 countries' refusal to sign an inadequate deal as "a sign of courage".
items.title: COP31 Climate Summit Ends Without a Global Agreement

items.summary: A family of smooth-coated otters (Lutrogale perspicillata), a species listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, is being spotted increasingly along Kuala Lumpur's Klang River, raising hopes that years of water-quality improvements are restoring urban wildlife habitat. The river was once one of the world's most polluted waterways, rated Class 5 (severely polluted) under Malaysia's ranking system; cleanup efforts have since improved it to Class 3 (moderately polluted). Malaysian wildlife ecologist Woo Chee Yoong attributed the otters' return to this improvement and noted that their presence indicates a functioning food web—where otters are found, fish exist, which signals a clean and healthy river. However, several details remain uncertain: experts do not know how many otter groups exist or how they move through the city, whether these animals have genuinely returned versus having been hidden in less visible urban environments before 2019 (when Woo first learned of them via local media), or why their numbers appear to be growing. To address this gap, MON—the conservation group co-founded by Woo—hopes to establish a citizen science system for reporting sightings.
items.title: Smooth-coated otters resurging along Kuala Lumpur's Klang River signal river cleanup progress

items.summary:
A post-midterm survey conducted by Precision Strategies and data firm Tunnl, titled Beyond the Manosphere: The Vote Moved Together. The Culture Didn't — examined American attitudes two years after what has been called the 'manosphere election.' The report found that Joe Rogan remains the most trusted media figure among men even as their electoral leanings shifted toward Democrats. Forty-nine percent of men said they trust Rogan, including 41% of Democratic-identifying men, a higher share than any other individual polled; no single person earned more than 22% of women's trust. Tunnl attributed part of this dynamic to the finding that 63% of men reported having no male role models in their lives, and noted that Rogan's longform interview format has inspired imitators ranging from Theo Von to the U.S. military.

The survey also found partisan divisions on media regulation: half of Republicans (51% of men, 50% of women) support government restriction of access for outlets deemed biased, while a slight majority of the overall population prioritized press access. On partisanship broadly, Americans — particularly Gen Z — shifted toward Democrats without developing lasting party loyalty amid ongoing economic concerns about job losses and financial hardship; 45% of men under age 30 identified as independents despite this Democratic swing.

The report also indicated growing weariness with certain MAGA cultural initiatives: only 16% of men and 11% of women said the Trump administration's anti-DEI efforts helped them, while most reported no difference. On gender roles, just 13% of women and 19% of men expressed a desire for more full-time homemakers — an incentive the Trump administration has pursued.

On AI usage, about one-fifth of respondents said they had used AI chatbots for companionship at higher rates among younger Americans; Asian, Black, and Hispanic respondents reported using AI more often than white Americans. Tunnl's Brent Seaborn characterized the landscape as shifting toward understanding who people trust rather than only what they believe.
items.title: Post-Midterms Report Finds Joe Rogan Remains Most Trusted Media Figure Among Men Despite Democratic Electoral Shift

Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has issued open tenders under Contract Package ORE/01 to procure renewable energy from an Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS)-connected project combining solar photovoltaic generation with a co-located Battery Energy Storage System (BESS). The tender follows a competitive bidding process, including an electronic reverse auction conducted online through the Central Public Procurement (CPP) e-tendering portal. A selected developer must complete the project within 15 months of receiving the Letter of Award and meet technical and financial qualification requirements set in the Request for Selection document.

The tender specifies a non-refundable tender document fee of ₹20,000 excluding GST, payable via RTGS, NEFT or IMPS. Bidders must also submit an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) of ₹23.9 crore as tender security, either electronically through the same payment channels from their own bank account—or for joint ventures/consortiums from a constituent member's account—or as an original Bank Guarantee or Fixed Deposit Receipt valid for at least 45 days beyond the 120-day tender validity period (extending to May 3, 2027).

The schedule runs through December 2026: tender document sale opened November 19 and closes December 10; pre-bid meeting registration by November 25 with the meeting held November 26 at Metro Bhawan's seventh-floor conference room (A Wing); clarification requests due November 27, with addenda issued by December 1. Online bid submission opens December 3 and closes December 10, coinciding with physical EMD delivery to the Senior General Manager (Contracts) office; technical bids open December 11 at 3:00 PM.

Bidders must register on the CPP portal using a valid Class-II or Class-III digital signature certificate issued to an authorised signatory. Financial bid opening and e-Reverse Auction dates will be announced separately for technically qualified bidders, with deviations from RfS conditions potentially resulting in rejection.
items.title: DMRC Invites Bids for ISTS-Connected Solar Project with Battery Storage
